<reason>Side B won a genuinely competitive debate. A's strongest weapon was the verification dilemma: B's own alternative (cash, respite, services) requires identifying real caregivers, so B cannot call the gate impossible. But B answered this cleanly and repeatedly with a principled distinction—a rough gate can support a temporary, stoppable benefit because "the error dies with the payment," while a credit vests, compounds, and bills future workers who never consented. A's counter that this is "a difference of degree, not kind" never broke that distinction, and B's closing image ("a check you can stop and a debt you cannot") crystallized it memorably. A also retreated from the opening's supplier/public-savings claim to a weaker "margin" argument, which B flagged and punished ("a margin somewhere cannot justify every piggybacked year"; if most care happens anyway, the credit is a vast transfer, not cheap). B answered both pressure questions directly with "Neither" plus reasons, maintained a coherent framework (pensions as deferred wages/insurance, not a moral ledger), and offered a constructive alternative that absorbed A's dignity rhetoric. A's execution costs—two clipped turns (opening and rebuttal 2)—compounded the burden, cutting off the final rebuttal's strongest sweep. A's best moments (the politically-drawn-line argument, the both-ways dilemma on fiscal exposure) landed but were contained. B made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was A's pressure question Q1 (verification contradiction) versus B's Rebuttal 2 response: benefits that are temporary, reviewable, and need-based can tolerate imperfect verification because errors expire with the payment, while pension credits permanently vest and compound claims against workers who never entered that household. This reframing dissolved A's sharpest attack and anchored B's entire closing.</best_rebuttal>
